extraction.name: Visual Question Answering: Datasets, Algorithms, and Future Challenges
extraction.description: A review paper that critically examines the current state of visual question answering in terms of problem formulation, existing datasets, evaluation metrics, and algorithms, with discussion of dataset limitations and future directions.
extraction.creator: Kushal Kafle and Christopher Kanan
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The paper reviews multiple existing VQA datasets and describes their collection methods, including manual crowdsourcing, automatic generation from captions, and synthetic scene generation.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Manual Human Curator, Software Collection, Experiments
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The reviewed VQA datasets use images from sources including NYU-DepthV2, COCO, Flickr100M/YFCC100M, and synthetic cartoon scenes.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: For COCO-QA, an NLP algorithm derives question-answer pairs from image captions, including breaking longer sentences into smaller chunks for processing.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: The reviewed datasets use human-generated questions and answers in several cases; for COCO-VQA, AMT workers generated questions to 'Stump a smart robot' and separate workers generated answers, with ten independent annotators answering each question.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The paper discusses disagreement and consensus-based evaluation, noting that multiple answers per question are used for consensus-based metrics and that inter-human agreement is limited for some question types.
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: For SYNTH-VQA, synthetic human models vary by age, gender, and races.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The paper discusses VQA as an aid for blind and visually impaired individuals and as a way to improve human-computer interaction.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The paper states that existing VQA datasets contain exploitable biases in question and answer distributions, including language bias and skewed yes/no answers, allowing models to perform well without truly solving VQA.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The paper identifies limitations including small dataset size, restricted scene diversity, grammatical errors from automatic QA generation, subjective questions without objective answers, low inter-human agreement, and biased evaluation.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The reviewed datasets are intended to train and evaluate VQA systems and benchmarks.

name.evidence: Visual Question Answering: Datasets, Algorithms, and Future Challenges

description.evidence: In this review, we critically examine the current state of VQA in terms of problem formulation, existing datasets, evaluation metrics, and algorithms.

creator.evidence: Kushal Kae and Christopher Kanan

inLanguage.evidence: We were unable to retrieve the English version of the dataset from provided download link.

isLiveDataset.evidence: In this review, we discuss existing datasets and methods for VQA.

rai:dataCollection.evidence: In the following subsections, we critically review the available datasets. We describe how the datasets were created and discuss their limitations.

rai:dataCollectionType.evidence: Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT) workers were employed to generate questions for each image by being asked to `Stump a smart robot,' and a separate pool of workers were hired to generate the answers to the questions. In COCO-QA [31], QA pairs are created for images using an Natural Language Processing (NLP) algorithm that derives them from the COCO image captions. SYNTH-VQA consists of 50,000 synthetic scenes that depict cartoon images in different simulated scenarios.

rai:dataCollectionRawData.evidence: With exception of DAQUAR, all of the datasets include images from the Microsoft Common Objects in Context (COCO) dataset [10]... Visual Genome and Visual7W use images from Flickr100M in addition to the COCO images. A portion of The VQA Dataset contains synthetic cartoon imagery, which we will refer to as SYNTH-VQA.

rai:dataCollectionTimeframe.evidence: Beginning in 2014, five major datasets for VQA have been publicly released.

rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol.evidence: In COCO-QA [31], QA pairs are created for images using an Natural Language Processing (NLP) algorithm that derives them from the COCO image captions. Longer sentences are broken into smaller chunks for ease of processing, but in many of these cases the algorithm does not cope well with the presence of clauses and grammatical variations in sentence formation.

rai:dataAnnotationProtocol.evidence: Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT) workers were employed to generate questions for each image by being asked to `Stump a smart robot,' and a separate pool of workers were hired to generate the answers to the questions. Each of the questions is then answered by 10 independent annotators.

rai:dataAnnotationPlatform.evidence: Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT) workers were employed to generate questions for each image by being asked to `Stump a smart robot,' and a separate pool of workers were hired to generate the answers to the questions.

rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis.evidence: The multiple answers per question are used in the consensus-based evaluation metric for the dataset, which is discussed in Section 4. Using Accuracy VQA, the inter-human agreement on COCO-VQA is only 83.3%.

rai:annotationsPerItem.evidence: COCO-VQA consists of three questions per image, with ten answers per question. Each of the questions is then answered by 10 independent annotators.

rai:personalSensitiveInformation.evidence: The models also span different age, gender, and races to provide variation in appearance.

rai:dataSocialImpact.evidence: The most immediate is as an aid to blind and visually impaired individuals, enabling them to get information about images both on the web and in the real world. More generally, VQA could be used to improve human-computer interaction as a natural way to query visual content.

rai:dataBiases.evidence: If a dataset contains easily exploitable biases in the distribution of the questions or answers, it may be possible for an algorithm to perform well on the dataset without really solving the VQA problem. Relatively simple image-blind algorithms have achieved 49.6% accuracy on COCO-VQA using the question alone.

rai:dataLimitations.evidence: While DAQUAR was a pioneering dataset for VQA, it is too small to successfully train and evaluate more complex models. This results in awkwardly phrased questions, with many containing grammatical errors, and others being completely unintelligible. The dataset also contains many subjective, opinion-seeking questions that do not have a single objective answer.

rai:dataUseCases.evidence: These datasets enable VQA systems to be trained and evaluated.
